{{Short description|Infinite prime numbers of the form a^2+b^4}}
[[File:John Friedlander at Oberwolfach 2008.jpg|thumb|John Friedlander]]
[[File:Henryk Iwaniec.JPG|thumb|Henryk Iwaniec]]
In [[analytic number theory]] the '''Friedlander–Iwaniec theorem''' states that there are infinitely many [[prime number]]s of the form <math>a^2 + b^4</math>. The first few such primes are

:2, 5, 17, 37, 41, 97, 101, 137, 181, 197, 241, 257, 277, 281, 337, 401, 457, 577, 617, 641, 661, 677, 757, 769, 821, 857, 881, 977, … {{OEIS|id=A028916}}.

The difficulty in this statement lies in the very sparse nature of this sequence: the number of integers of the form <math>a^2+b^4</math> less than <math>X</math> is roughly of the order <math>X^{3/4}</math>.

==History==
The theorem was proved in 1997 by [[John Friedlander]] and [[Henryk Iwaniec]].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Friedlander |first1=John |last2=Iwaniec |first2=Henryk |year=1997 |title=Using a parity-sensitive sieve to count prime values of a polynomial |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|PNAS]] |volume=94 |issue=4 |pages=1054–1058 |doi=10.2307/121034 
|doi-access=free }}.</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Friedlander |first1=John |last2=Iwaniec |first2=Henryk |year=1998 |title= The polynomial <math>X^2 + Y^4</math> captures its primes |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |volume=148 |issue=3 |pages=945–1040 |doi=10.2307/121034
|doi-access=free }}.</ref> Iwaniec was awarded the 2001 [[Ostrowski Prize]] in part for his contributions to this work.<ref name=ostrowski>[https://www.ams.org/notices/200207/comm-ostrowski.pdf "Iwaniec, Sarnak, and Taylor Receive Ostrowski Prize"]</ref>

==Refinements==

The theorem was refined by [[Heath-Brown|D.R. Heath-Brown]] and [[Xiannan Li]] in 2017.<ref>{{Citation| last1=Heath-Brown|first1=D.R. |last2=Li|first2=Xiannan|year=2017|title=Prime values of <math>a^2 + p^4</math>|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] | volume=208|pages=441–499|doi=10.1007/s00222-016-0694-0}}.</ref> In particular, they proved that the polynomial <math>a^2 + b^4</math> represents infinitely many primes when the variable <math>b</math> is also required to be prime. Namely, if <math>f(n)</math> is the prime numbers less than <math>n</math> in the form <math>a^2 + b^4,</math> then

<math>f(n) \sim v \frac{x^{3/4}}{\log{x}}</math>

where

<math>v=2 \sqrt{\pi} \frac{\Gamma(5/4)}{\Gamma(7/4)} \prod_{p \equiv 1\bmod 4} \frac{p-2}{p-1} \prod_{p \equiv 3\bmod 4} \frac{p}{p-1}.</math>

In 2024, a paper by [[Stanley Yao Xiao]]<ref>{{Citation |last=Xiao |first=Stanley Yao |year=2024 |title=Prime values of <math>f(a,b^2)</math> and <math>f(a,p^2)</math>, <math>f</math> quadratic |journal=[[Algebra and Number Theory]] |volume=18 |issue=9 |pages=1619–1679 |doi=10.2140/ant.2024.18.1619  |arxiv=2111.04136 }}</ref> generalized the Friedlander—Iwaniec theorem and Heath-Brown—Li theorems to general binary quadratic forms, including indefinite forms. In particular one has, for <math>f(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}[x,y]</math> a positive definite [[binary quadratic form]] satisfying <math>f(x,1) \not \equiv x(x+1) \pmod{2} </math>, one has, for <math> \lambda </math> the prime [[indicator function]] and

<math> \mathfrak{S}_f = \operatorname{Area} \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : f(x,y^2) \leq 1\}</math>

and

<math> \nu_f = \prod_{p \nmid \Delta(f)} \left(1 - \frac{\rho_f(p)}{p} \right) \left(1 - \frac{1}{p} \right)^{-1} \prod_{p | \Delta(f)} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p} \right)^{-1}, </math>

with <math> \rho_f(m) = \# \{x \pmod{m} : f(x,1) \equiv 0 \pmod{m}\}</math>, the asymptotic formula:

<math> \sum_{\begin{array}{c}
m, \ell \in \mathbb{Z}\\
f(m,\ell^2) \leq X
\end{array}
} \lambda(f(m, \ell^2)) = \frac{\nu_f \mathfrak{S}_f X^{3/4}}{\log X}\left(1 + O \left(\frac{\log \log X}{\log X} \right) \right) </math>

Here <math>\Delta(f) </math> is the [[discriminant]] of the quadratic form <math>f </math>.

For indefinite, irreducible forms <math> f(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}[x,y]</math> satisfying <math> f(x,1) \not \equiv x(x+1) \pmod{2} </math>, put

<math> \mathfrak{S}_f = \lim_{X \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\operatorname{Area}\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : 0< f(x,y^2) \leq X, 0 < y < X^{1/4} }{X^{3/4}}.</math>

Then one has the asymptotic formula

<math> \sum_{\begin{array}{c}
m, \ell \in \mathbb{Z}\\
f(m,\ell^2) \leq X \\ 0 < \ell \leq X^{3/4}
\end{array}
} \lambda (f(m, \ell^2)) = \frac{\nu_f \mathfrak{S}_f X^{3/4}}{\log X} \left(1 + O \left(\frac{\log \log X}{\log X} \right) \right).
</math>

==Special case==
When {{math|1=''b'' = 1}}, the Friedlander–Iwaniec primes have the form <math>a^2+1</math>, forming the set
:2, 5, 17, 37, 101, 197, 257, 401, 577, 677, 1297, 1601, 2917, 3137, 4357, 5477, 7057, 8101, 8837, 12101, 13457, 14401, 15377, … {{OEIS|id=A002496}}.

It is conjectured  (one of [[Landau's problems]]) that this set is infinite. However, this is not implied by the Friedlander–Iwaniec theorem.
